claim: 16 participants volunteered to participate in the experiment, with 8 in the tibialis anterior (TA) experiment (age: 27 ± 3) and 8 in the vastus lateralis (VL) experiment (age: 27 ± 10).
source: 16 young individuals volunteered to participate either in the experiment on the TA (n=8; age: 27 ± 3) or on the VL (n=8; age: 27 ± 10).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of participants, their age, and group assignments.

claim: The study was approved by Imperial College London (Study 18IC4685) and Comité de Protection des Personnes Ouest III (Study 23.00453.000166).
source: The study was reviewed and approved by Imperial College London (Study 18IC4685) and Comité de Protection des Personnes Ouest III (Study 23.00453.000166) and followed the standards of the declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the ethical approval bodies and study numbers.

claim: The average number of motor units identified in each contraction per participant was 42 ± 24 (up to 95) for TA and 33 ± 15 (up to 71) for VL.
source: The average number of motor units identified in each contraction per participant was 42 ± 24 (25th–75th percentile: 24–53, up to 95; Table 1) motor units from the TA and 33 ± 15 (25th–75th percentile: 23–47, up to 71; Table 1) motor units from the VL.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data on motor unit identification.

claim: The proportion of EMG signal represented by identified motor units was 69.3 ± 17.3% for TA and 55.2 ± 19.5% for VL.
source: The ratio between the powers of synthetic and experimental EMG signals was calculated (Figure 1B): it was 69.3 ± 17.3% (25th–75th percentile: 59.3–83.6%, up to 94.2%) for TA and 55.2 ± 19.5% (25th–75th percentile: 50.0–71.9%, up to 86.5%) for VL (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on signal reconstruction and references Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: On average, 67.1 ± 10.0% of motor units were tracked between consecutive target forces for TA and 57.2 ± 5.1% for VL.
source: On average, we tracked 67.1 ± 10.0% (25th–75th percentile: 53.9–80.1%) of the motor units between consecutive target forces (10% increments, e.g. between 10% and 20% MVC) for TA and 57.2 ± 5.1% (25th–75th percentile: 46.6–68.3%) of the motor units for VL (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for motor unit tracking success.

claim: In total, 129 ± 44 motor units per participant were identified in TA and 130 ± 63 motor units per participant in VL.
source: In total, we identified 129 ± 44 motor units (25th–75th percentile: 100–164, up to 194) per participant in TA and 130 ± 63 motor units (25th–75th percentile: 103–173, up to 199) per participant in VL.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the total number of motor units identified per participant.

claim: 92.1% of motor units in TA and 87.0% in VL had a lower RMSE between target forces compared with other motor units, confirming their uniqueness.
source: Inspection of the data for each motor unit revealed that 92.1% (TA) and 87.0% (VL) of the motor units had a lower RMSE between target forces compared with the other motor units (<5th percentile).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages demonstrating motor unit uniqueness.

claim: 69.5% of motor units in TA and 72.3% in VL had input-output functions better fitted by a natural logarithm function.
source: The result was that 69.5% of the motor units in TA and 72.3% of those in VL had an input-output function better fitted by a natural logarithm (Figure 2B, inset panels).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for the best-fit function type.

claim: The initial acceleration of firing rate was significantly greater for low-threshold motor units (1.0 ± 0.7 pps²) than medium-threshold motor units (0.6 ± 0.3 pps²) in TA.
source: The initial acceleration of firing rate in TA was greater for the low- (1.0 ± 0.7 pps2; p<0.001) and the high- (1.0 ± 0.3 pps2; p=0.032) threshold motor units than for medium-threshold motor units (0.6 ± 0.3 pps2), with no difference between the low- and high-threshold motor units (p=0.999; Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical values and statistical comparisons.

claim: The initial acceleration of firing rate was greater for low-threshold motor units (0.6 ± 0.6 pps²) than for medium-threshold (0.4 ± 0.2 pps²) and high-threshold motor units (0.4 ± 0.2 pps²) in VL.
source: Similarly, the initial acceleration of firing rate was greater for low-threshold motor units (0.6 ± 0.6 pps2) than for medium- (0.4 ± 0.2 pps2; p<0.001) and high-threshold motor units (0.4 ± 0.2 pps2; p=0.013) in VL, with no difference between the medium- and high-threshold motor units (p=0.990; Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical values and statistical comparisons.

claim: The rate of increase in firing rate was significantly greater for TA (3.5 ± 1.7 pps) than for VL (2.0 ± 1.1 pps).
source: The rate of increase was significantly greater for TA (3.5 ± 1.7 pps; 25th–75th percentile: 2.4–4.1 pps) than for VL (2.0 ± 1.1 pps; 25th–75th percentile: 1.3–2.6 pps. p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical values and statistical comparison.

claim: Most motor units (92.0% in TA and 80.9% in VL) increased firing rates by more than one pulse per second between contractions.
source: Most motor units (92.0% in TA and 80.9% in VL) increased firing rates by more than one pulse per second between contractions up to the maximal force tested or until tracking was not possible.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for motor unit firing rate increases.

claim: Only medium-threshold motor units exhibited significant positive hysteresis in both muscles (TA: –3.8 ± 7.2 pps; p=0.013; VL: –3.1 ± 6.0 pps; p=0.026).
source: The result was that only medium-threshold motor units had a significant positive hysteresis (derecruitment threshold was lower) in both muscles (TA: –3.8 ± 7.2 pps; p=0.013; VL: –3.1 ± 6.0 pps; p=0.026), whereas low-threshold motor units from both muscles (TA: –1.5 ± 4.8; VL: –1.0 ± 3.2 pps; p>0.221) did not exhibit significant hysteresis.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical values and statistical significance for hysteresis.

claim: High-threshold motor units from VL exhibited a negative hysteresis (+3.2 ± 6.7 pps; p=0.039), indicating that derecruitment threshold was greater than recruitment threshold.
source: Although high-threshold motor units from TA followed the same trend (–1.7 ± 6.0 pps; p<0.437), high-threshold motor units from VL exhibited a negative hysteresis (VL: +3.2 ± 6.7 pps; p=0.039), which indicated that derecruitment threshold was greater than the recruitment threshold.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical values and statistical significance for negative hysteresis.

claim: Most motor units (TA: 60.2%; VL: 76.7%) were best fit with the same relation during both ramp-up and ramp-down phases.
source: Most motor units (TA: 60.2%; VL: 76.7%) were best fit with the same relation during the two phases.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for consistency of fit between phases.

claim: The motor unit is a unique structure comprising an alpha motoneuron and the muscle fibres it innervates.
source: This versatility relies on a unique structure that converts neural inputs into muscle force; i.e., the motor unit, which comprises an alpha motoneuron and the muscle fibres it innervates (Sherrington, 1925; Heckman and Enoka, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature defining the motor unit structure.

claim: The nervous system controls muscle force by modulating the number of active motor units (recruitment) and their firing rates (rate coding).
source: The nervous system controls muscle force by modulating the number of active motor units (recruitment) and their firing rates (rate coding; Enoka and Duchateau, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on motor control mechanisms.

claim: Motor units are recruited in a fixed order following the size principle.
source: This control strategy involves projecting a substantial level of common excitatory synaptic inputs to motoneurons (Farina et al., 2014b; Farina and Negro, 2015; Negro et al., 2016b) that recruits them in a fixed order following the size principle (Henneman, 1957).
evidence: The manuscript cites Henneman's size principle as established knowledge.

claim: Animal studies have shown two stages in the rate coding of individual motor units: amplification and rate limiting.
source: Animal studies have shown two stages in the rate coding of individual motor units to increase muscle force (amplification and rate limiting) in response to linear increases in the net excitatory synaptic inputs (Bennett et al., 1998a; Lee and Heckman, 2000; Powers and Binder, 2001; Binder et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple animal studies demonstrating two-stage rate coding.

claim: The two stages of rate coding represent different responses of motoneurons to ionotropic inputs due to modulation of their intrinsic properties by metabotropic inputs.
source: These stages represent the different responses of motoneurons to ionotropic inputs due to modulation of their intrinsic properties by metabotropic inputs acting on the somato-dendritic surfaces of motoneurons through several ion channels (Powers and Binder, 2001; Heckman and Enoka, 2012; Binder et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature explaining the mechanistic basis of two-stage rate coding.

claim: Similar characteristics in firing activity have been observed in humans, although limited to small samples of motor units (typically <40) over narrow force ranges (typically <30% MVC).
source: Similar characteristics in firing activity have been observed in humans (Fuglevand et al., 2015; Revill and Fuglevand, 2017; Beauchamp et al., 2023), although these observations have been limited to small samples of motor units (typically <40) with firing activities experimentally decoded over a narrow range of submaximal forces (typically <30% maximal voluntary contraction [MVC] force; Fuglevand et al., 2015; Revill and Fuglevand, 2017; Beauchamp et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript cites human studies and notes their limitations.

claim: The motoneuron pools of TA and VL receive a large part of common input, constraining the recruitment of their motor units in a fixed order across tasks.
source: The motoneuron pools of these two muscles of the lower limb receive a large part of common input (Laine et al., 2015; Negro et al., 2016b), constraining the recruitment of their motor units in a fixed order across tasks.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on common input to these muscles.

claim: The ramp-up and ramp-down phases were performed at a constant rate of 5% MVC·s⁻¹.
source: They were performed at a constant rate of 5% MVC·s–1 and the force plateau was maintained for either 10 s (70–80% MVC), 15 s (50–60% MVC), or 20 s (10–40% MVC) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the rate of force change during ramps.

claim: The force plateau was maintained for either 10 s (70–80% MVC), 15 s (50–60% MVC), or 20 s (10–40% MVC).
source: They were performed at a constant rate of 5% MVC·s–1 and the force plateau was maintained for either 10 s (70–80% MVC), 15 s (50–60% MVC), or 20 s (10–40% MVC) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the duration of force plateaus at different intensities.

claim: The target force during the plateau ranged from 10% to 80% MVC in increments of 10% MVC in randomized order.
source: The target during the plateau ranged from 10% to 80% MVC in increments of 10% MVC (randomised order).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental protocol.

claim: EMG signals were recorded from TA or VL using four arrays of 64 surface electrodes (256 electrodes per muscle).
source: 16 participants performed either isometric dorsiflexion (n=8) or knee extension tasks (n=8) while we recorded the EMG activity of the tibialis anterior (TA - dorsiflexion) or the vastus lateralis (VL - knee extension) with four arrays of 64 surface electrodes (256 electrodes per muscle).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the recording setup.

claim: According to previous estimates, the number of motor units detectable with surface EMG would be 200 ± 61 for TA and 146 ± 29 for VL.
source: According to previous estimates, the number of motor units detectable with surface EMG in human would be 200 ± 61 for TA and 146 ± 29 for VL (Duchateau and Enoka, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous estimates of detectable motor units.

claim: The fast initial acceleration stage reflects the amplification of synaptic inputs through the activation of persistent inward currents via voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels.
source: The fast initial acceleration stage reflects the amplification of synaptic inputs through the activation of persistent inward currents via voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels (Bennett et al., 1998a; Lee and Heckman, 2000; Heckman and Enoka, 2012; Binder et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature explaining the mechanism of initial acceleration.

claim: The influence of neuromodulatory inputs is greater during the initial acceleration phase for low- than for high-threshold motor units, presumably due to a larger ratio between the amplitude of inward currents and the input conductance in low-threshold motoneurons.
source: Although noradrenergic and serotonergic synapses that generate persistent inward currents are widespread within motor unit pools (Maratta et al., 2015), the influence of the neuromodulatory inputs is greater during this phase for low- than for high-threshold motor units. This is presumably due to a larger ratio between the amplitude of inward currents and the input conductance in low-threshold motoneurons (Huh et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature and provides mechanistic reasoning.

claim: The level of recurrent and reciprocal inhibition has probably increased with the increase in force during the ramp-up, progressively blunting the effect of persistent inward currents for late-recruited motor units.
source: The level of recurrent and reciprocal inhibition has also probably increased with the increase in force during the ramp-up, progressively blunting the effect of persistent inward currents for late-recruited motor units (Kuo et al., 2003; Hyngstrom et al., 2007; Revill and Fuglevand, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature and provides mechanistic reasoning with speculative language ('probably').

claim: The integration of larger inhibitory inputs should linearise the firing rate/force relation.
source: This may also explain the larger percentage of high-threshold motor units with a linear fit for the firing rate/force relation (Figure 2), as the integration of larger inhibitory inputs should linearise the firing rate/force relation (Revill and Fuglevand, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature and provides mechanistic reasoning.

claim: The second stage of rate coding corresponds to mechanisms previously referred to as 'rate limiting' or 'saturation'.
source: This stage corresponds to mechanisms previously referred to as 'rate limiting' (Heckman and Binder, 1993; Heckman and Enoka, 2012; Powers and Heckman, 2017) or 'saturation' (De Luca and Contessa, 2012; Fuglevand et al., 2015), and was more pronounced for low- than high-threshold motor units (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature defining the second stage of rate coding.

claim: The difference in rate limiting between low- and high-threshold motor units may be explained by smaller excitatory synaptic inputs onto low- than high-threshold motoneurons.
source: This difference may be explained by smaller excitatory synaptic inputs onto low- than high-threshold motoneurons (Powers and Binder, 2001; Heckman and Enoka, 2012), lower synaptic driving potential of the dendritic membrane (Powers and Binder, 2000; Cushing et al., 2005; Fuglevand et al., 2015), and longer and larger afterhyperpolarisation phase in low- than high-threshold motoneurons (Bakels and Kernell, 1993; Gardiner, 1993; Deardorff et al., 2013; Caillet et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies providing mechanistic explanations.

claim: While the size of the motor unit determines its recruitment threshold, neuromodulatory inputs determine its gain.
source: While the size of the motor unit determines its recruitment threshold, neuromodulatory inputs determine its gain.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes findings to make this interpretive claim.

claim: In a similar fashion as size imposes a fixed recruitment order, neuromodulatory inputs determine a spectrum of variations in motor unit firing rates without the need to differentiate the ionotropic inputs to each motoneuron.
source: Thus, in a similar fashion as size imposes a fixed recruitment order (Henneman, 1957), neuromodulatory inputs determine a spectrum of variations in motor unit firing rates without the need to differentiate the ionotropic inputs to each motoneuron. (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 3; Powers and Heckman, 2017; Bräcklein et al., 2022; Chardon et al., 2024; Škarabot et al., 2023b).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature and references figures to support this interpretive claim.

claim: Because high-threshold motor units exhibit a higher gain than low-threshold motor units, their firing rate could eventually reach similar or even greater values than that of low-threshold motor units during strong contractions.
source: Because high-threshold motor units exhibit a higher gain than low-threshold motor units (Figure 3), their firing rate could eventually reach similar or even greater values than that of low-threshold motor units during strong contractions (Gydikov and Kosarov, 1974; Moritz et al., 2005; Oya et al., 2009; Škarabot et al., 2023b).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature and references data to support this inference.

claim: The onion skin principle may not hold in all muscles and for all contraction forces.
source: This indicates that the onion skin principle (De Luca and Contessa, 2012; De Luca and Contessa, 2015) may not hold in all muscles and for all contraction forces (Gydikov and Kosarov, 1974; Moritz et al., 2005; Oya et al., 2009; Škarabot et al., 2023b).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this interpretive claim.

claim: Rate coding patterns should vary with the pattern of contractions, with fast contractions lowering the range of recruitment thresholds within motoneuron pools.
source: In addition, rate coding patterns should also vary with the pattern of contractions, with fast contractions lowering the range of recruitment thresholds within motoneuron pools (Desmedt and Godaux, 1977b; Desmedt and Godaux, 1979; van Bolhuis et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this claim about contraction pattern effects.

claim: The variability in rate coding observed between motor units from the same pool could lead to small deviations from the size principle sometimes observed between pairs of units during isometric contractions.
source: The variability in rate coding observed here between motor units from the same pool could lead to small deviations from the size principle sometimes observed between pairs of units during isometric contractions with various patterns of force (Desmedt and Godaux, 1979; Marshall et al., 2022) or during the derecruitment phase (Bräcklein et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this interpretive claim.

claim: The hysteresis is possible because of the bistability of the membrane potential mediated by inward currents from calcium channels.
source: This hysteresis is possible because of the bistability of the membrane potential mediated by inward currents from calcium channels, the two stable membrane states being the resting potential, and a depolarised state that enables self-sustained firing (Hounsgaard et al., 1988; Lee and Heckman, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature explaining the mechanism of hysteresis.

claim: The absence of statistically significant hysteresis in low-threshold motoneurons may be explained by their early recruitment during the first percentages of force, mathematically lowering the potential amplitude of their hysteresis.
source: The absence of statistically significant hysteresis in low-threshold motoneurons may be simply explained by their early recruitment during the first percentages of force, mathematically lowering the potential amplitude of their hysteresis.
evidence: The manuscript provides a mechanistic explanation for the absence of hysteresis.

claim: Prominent outward currents may attenuate the impact of persistent inward currents on the prolongation of firing activity in low-threshold motoneurons.
source: Alternatively, prominent outward currents may attenuate the impact of persistent inward currents on the prolongation of their firing activity (Powers and Heckman, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to provide an alternative mechanistic explanation.

claim: The absence of hysteresis (TA) and negative hysteresis (VL) in high-threshold motoneurons can be explained by a briefer membrane bistability due to a faster decay of inward currents from calcium channels, and a narrower range of membrane depolarisation over which these inward currents are activated.
source: Similarly, the absence of hysteresis (TA) and even a negative hysteresis (VL) in high-threshold motoneurons can be explained by a briefer membrane bistability due to a faster decay of inward currents from calcium channels, and a narrower range of membrane depolarisation over which these inward currents are activated (Lee and Heckman, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to provide a mechanistic explanation.

claim: The difference in rate coding between TA and VL may reflect a varying balance between excitatory/inhibitory synaptic inputs and neuromodulation due to multiple spinal circuits.
source: This difference may reflect a varying balance between excitatory/inhibitory synaptic inputs and neuromodulation due to multiple spinal circuits (Heckman and Binder, 1993; Heckman et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2017; Powers and Heckman, 2017; Chardon et al., 2024; Škarabot et al., 2023b).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this mechanistic interpretation.

claim: The strength of recurrent and reciprocal inhibitory inputs to motoneurons innervating VL and TA, and their proportional or inverse covariation with excitatory inputs, may explain the differences in rate limiting and maximal firing rates.
source: Specifically, the strength of recurrent and reciprocal inhibitory inputs to motoneurons innervating VL and TA, and their proportional or inverse covariation with excitatory inputs, respectively, may explain the differences in rate limiting and maximal firing rates (Heckman and Binder, 1993; Heckman et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2017; Powers and Heckman, 2017; Chardon et al., 2024; Škarabot et al., 2023b).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this mechanistic interpretation.

claim: The motor units from the VL may receive more recurrent inhibition than those of distal muscles, though direct evidence of these differences remains to be found in humans.
source: Thus, the motor units from the VL may receive more recurrent inhibition than those of distal muscles, though direct evidence of these differences remains to be found in humans (Windhorst, 1996).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature and acknowledges the speculative nature of this claim.

claim: Similar differences in rate coding were previously observed between proximal and distal muscles of the upper limb.
source: Interestingly, similar differences in rate coding were previously observed between proximal and distal muscles of the upper limb (De Luca et al., 1982).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this comparative observation.

claim: Muscles from the face have different rate coding characteristics with much higher firing rates.
source: However, other muscles that serve different functions within the human body, such as muscles from the face, have different rate coding characteristics with much higher firing rates (Kirk et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to note differences in other muscle types.

claim: The accurate control of force depends on the firing activity of the population of active motor units, which effectively filters out the synaptic noise of individual motor units and primarily transforms common synaptic inputs into muscle force.
source: The accurate control of force depends on the firing activity of the population of active motor units, which effectively filters out the synaptic noise of individual motor units and primarily transforms common synaptic inputs into muscle force (Dideriksen et al., 2012; Farina et al., 2014b; Farina and Negro, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this claim about force control.

claim: The bandwidth of muscle force is <10 Hz during isometric contractions.
source: Because the bandwidth of muscle force is <10 Hz during isometric contractions (Enoka and Farina, 2021), the activation of inward currents to low-threshold motoneurons at recruitment may enable them to promptly discharge at a rate (>8 pps) that transmits the effective common synaptic inputs (<8–10 Hz) without phase distortion (Dideriksen et al., 2012; Farina et al., 2014b; Farina and Negro, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this claim about force bandwidth.

claim: The activation of inward currents to low-threshold motoneurons at recruitment may enable them to promptly discharge at a rate (>8 pps) that transmits the effective common synaptic inputs (<8–10 Hz) without phase distortion.
source: Because the bandwidth of muscle force is <10 Hz during isometric contractions (Enoka and Farina, 2021), the activation of inward currents to low-threshold motoneurons at recruitment may enable them to promptly discharge at a rate (>8 pps) that transmits the effective common synaptic inputs (<8–10 Hz) without phase distortion (Dideriksen et al., 2012; Farina et al., 2014b; Farina and Negro, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Force generation can be described as the filtering of the cumulative firing activity of active motor units with the average twitch force of their muscle units.
source: Moreover, force generation can be described as the filtering of the cumulative firing activity of active motor units with the average twitch force of their muscle units (Farina and Negro, 2015; Thompson et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this conceptual framework.

claim: At low forces, recruitment of new motor units has a higher impact on force modulation than rate coding since each recruitment impacts both the cumulative firing activity of the pool and the average twitch force.
source: From this perspective, at low forces, recruitment of new motor units has a higher impact on force modulation than rate coding since each recruitment impacts both the cumulative firing activity of the pool and the average twitch force. Rate coding only modulates the cumulative firing activity.
evidence: The manuscript provides mechanistic reasoning based on the cited framework.

claim: The amplification of the firing rate of low-threshold motor units near their recruitment threshold instantly favours rate coding over the recruitment of additional motor units, which likely allows for smoother force control.
source: Thus, the amplification of the firing rate of low-threshold motor units near their recruitment threshold instantly favours rate coding over the recruitment of additional motor units, which likely allows for smoother force control.
evidence: The manuscript provides mechanistic reasoning with speculative language ('likely').

claim: The progressive recruitment of motor units with a higher gain promotes faster changes in firing rates, which promotes force control accuracy across the full force range.
source: Similarly, the progressive recruitment of motor units with a higher gain promotes faster changes in firing rates, which promotes force control accuracy across the full force range.
evidence: The manuscript provides mechanistic reasoning based on the observed data.

claim: The steep increase in firing rate over the first percentages of the ramp-up may enable the motor units to produce the required level of force despite having a more compliant muscle-tendon unit.
source: On a different note, the steep increase in firing rate over the first percentages of the ramp-up may also enable the motor units to produce the required level of force despite having a more compliant muscle-tendon unit (Mazzo et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature and provides mechanistic reasoning with speculative language ('may').

claim: Participants had no history of lower limb injury in the last 6 months before the experiments nor lower leg pain that would impair their ability to complete the experimental tasks.
source: They had neither history of lower limb injury in the last 6 months before the experiments nor lower leg pain that would impair their ability to complete the experimental tasks.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: Participants provided their informed written consent before starting the experimental session.
source: Participants provided their informed written consent before starting the experimental session.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the consent procedure.

claim: For the ankle dorsiflexion session, participants sat with hips flexed at 45° and knees fully extended, with the foot positioned at 30° plantarflexion.
source: For the session of ankle dorsiflexions, participants sat on a massage table with the hips flexed at 45°, 0° being the hip neutral position, and the knees fully extended. The foot of the dominant leg (right in all participants) was fixed onto the pedal of an ankle dynamometer (OT Bioelettronica, Turin, Italy) positioned at 30° in the plantarflexion direction, 0° being the foot perpendicular to the shank.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental setup.

claim: For the knee extension session, participants sat with hips flexed at 85° and knees flexed at 85°.
source: For the session of knee extensions, participants sat on an instrumented chair with the hips flexed at 85°, 0° being the hip neutral position, and the knees flexed at 85°, 0° being the knees fully extended.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental setup.

claim: Participants performed two MVC with 2 min of rest in between.
source: Then, participants performed two MVC with 2 min of rest in between.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the MVC protocol.

claim: The contractions were separated by 90 s of rest and their order was randomised.
source: The contractions were separated by 90 s of rest and their order was randomised.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the rest period and randomization.

claim: EMG signals were recorded in monopolar derivation with a sampling frequency of 2048 Hz for surface electrodes and 10,240 Hz for intramuscular electrodes.
source: EMG signals were recorded in monopolar derivation with a sampling frequency of 2048 Hz for surface electrodes, 10,240 Hz for intramuscular electrodes, amplified (×150), band-pass filtered (10–500 Hz for surface; 100–4400 Hz for intramuscular), and digitised using a 400 channels acquisition system with a 16-bit resolution (EMG-Quattrocento; OT Bioelettronica, Italy).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the EMG recording parameters.

claim: The monopolar EMG signals were band-pass filtered between 20 and 500 Hz with a second-order Butterworth filter.
source: The monopolar EMG signals were band-pass filtered between 20 and 500 Hz with a second-order Butterworth filter, and channels with low signal-to-noise ratio or artefacts were discarded after visual inspection.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the signal processing steps.

claim: A source-separation algorithm was applied to the EMG signals to extract motor unit pulse trains, from which discharge times were automatically identified.
source: A source-separation algorithm (Farina and Holobar, 2016; Negro et al., 2016a) was applied to the EMG signals to extract motor unit pulse trains, from which discharge times were automatically identified.
evidence: The manuscript cites the algorithm and describes its application.

claim: All identified motor unit firings were visually inspected and manually edited when necessary.
source: All identified motor unit firings were visually inspected and manually edited when necessary (Avrillon et al., 2024).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the quality control procedure.

claim: Two discharge times were considered as common when they occurred within a time interval of 0.5 ms, and two or more motor units were considered as duplicates when they had at least 30% of their identified discharge times in common.
source: For this purpose, the pulse trains of pairs of motor units were first aligned using a cross-correlation function to account for a potential delay due to the propagation time of action potentials along the fibres. Then, two discharge times identified from these pulse trains were considered as common when they occurred within a time interval of 0.5 ms, and two or more motor units were considered as duplicates when they had at least 30% of their identified discharge times in common (Holobar et al., 2010; Negro et al., 2016a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the duplicate detection criteria.

claim: A threshold of 30% for duplicate detection is highly conservative and ensures the removal of all motor units with a level of synchronisation well above physiological values.
source: In principle, the limited level of synchronisation between individual motor units results in a few simultaneous discharge times between pairs of motor units. A threshold of 30% is therefore highly conservative and ensure the removal of all motor units with a level of synchronisation well above physiological values.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning for the chosen threshold.

claim: When duplicates were identified, the motor unit with the lowest coefficient of variation of the inter-spike intervals was retained for the analyses.
source: When duplicates were identified, the motor unit with the lowest coefficient of variation of the inter-spike intervals was retained for the analyses.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the selection criterion for duplicates.

claim: The manual editing was only accepted when the silhouette value increased or stayed well above the threshold of 0.9.
source: Then, the manual editing was only accepted when the silhouette value increased or stayed well above the threshold of 0.9 quantified with the silhouette value (Negro et al., 2016a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the quality control criterion for manual editing.

claim: For the simulation validation, a pool of 150 motor units was simulated producing forces from 10% to 80% of maximal excitation.
source: For the simulation, we generated the series of discharge times of a group of 150 motor units in an anatomical model entailing a cylindrical muscle volume with parallel fibres (see Konstantin et al., 2020, for a full description of the model), in which subcutaneous and skin layers separate the muscle from the surface electrodes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the simulation parameters and cites the model.

claim: The rate of agreement between simulated and estimated series of motor unit discharge times was calculated as the ratio between correctly identified discharge times and the sum of correctly identified discharge times, missed discharge times, and falsely identified discharge times.
source: Following this, we estimated the rate of agreements between simulated and estimated series of motor unit discharge times, calculated as the ratio between correctly identified discharge times and the sum of correctly identified discharge times, missed discharge times, and falsely identified discharge times.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the validation metric.

claim: For two-source validation, two motor units identified with intramuscular and surface EMG decompositions were considered as matches when they had at least 30% of their discharge times in common.
source: After the decomposition of both intramuscular and surface EMG signals, identified motor units were matched following the same procedure as for the elimination of duplicates. In short, the motor unit pulse trains were first aligned using a cross-correlation function. Two motor units identified with intramuscular and surface EMG decompositions were considered as matches when they had at least 30% of their discharge times in common.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the matching criterion for two-source validation.

claim: Motor units were tracked by projecting EMG signals from higher contraction levels onto separation vectors identified at lower contraction levels.
source: In this study, motor units were tracked by slightly adapting this process. First, EMG signals from two successive contraction levels, say 10% and 20% MVC, were separately decomposed. The motor unit pulse trains, the identified discharge times, and the associated separation vectors were saved for each contraction level. Second, the EMG signals from the highest contraction level (20% MVC) were projected onto the separation vectors identified in the lowest contraction level (10% MVC).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the tracking methodology.

claim: New series of discharge times were matched with those initially identified using >30% of common discharge times as the criterion.
source: Third, these new series of discharge times were matched with those that have been initially identified at 20% MVC using the same approach as during two-source validation (>30% of common discharge times, see above).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the matching criterion for tracking.

claim: Motor units with the highest reference RMSE values (>95th percentile) were considered as outliers due to tracking errors and were excluded from subsequent analyses.
source: Of note, motor units with the highest reference values (>95th percentile) were considered as outliers due to tracking errors and were excluded from the subsequent analyses (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the exclusion criterion.

claim: 34 motor units from TA and 28 from VL were excluded due to tracking errors.
source: We excluded 34 motor units from TA and 28 from VL.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of excluded motor units.

claim: The linear increase in force was assumed to reflect a proportional increase in the net synaptic excitatory inputs received by the motoneurons.
source: The linear increase in force was assumed to reflect a proportional increase in the net synaptic excitatory inputs received by the motoneurons, as proposed previously (Fuglevand et al., 1993; Revill and Fuglevand, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this assumption.

claim: Any deviation from a linear increase in firing rate with respect to a linear increase in force presumably reflects the influence of neuromodulatory inputs on motoneuron gain or a saturation of the motoneuron firing rate.
source: Thus, any deviation from a linear increase in firing rate with respect to a linear increase in force presumably reflects the influence of neuromodulatory inputs on motoneuron gain (Johnson et al., 2017; Revill and Fuglevand, 2017; Beauchamp et al., 2023), or a saturation of the motoneuron firing rate (Fuglevand et al., 2015; Revill and Fuglevand, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this interpretive assumption.

claim: The best model of the firing rate-force relation was determined as the fit with the lowest Bayesian information criterion (BIC).
source: The best model of the firing rate-force relation during the ramp-up phase was the fit with the lowest Bayesian information criterion (BIC).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the model selection criterion.

claim: The BIC assesses the performance of a model by balancing its goodness of fit with its complexity (number of parameters).
source: This criterion assesses the performance of a model by balancing its goodness of fit with its complexity (number of parameters).
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for using BIC.

claim: The initial acceleration of firing rate was calculated as the value of the first derivative of the natural logarithm function at the recruitment threshold.
source: The initial acceleration of the firing rate, likely due to the amplification of synaptic inputs by persistent inward currents (Lee and Heckman, 2000), was calculated as the value of the first derivative of the natural logarithm function at the recruitment threshold (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the calculation method and cites supporting literature.

claim: Motor units were clustered into three groups with equal ranges of recruitment thresholds: low- (0–25% MVC), medium- (25–50% MVC), and high- (50–75% MVC) threshold motor units.
source: Motor units were clustered into three groups with equal ranges of recruitment thresholds: low- (0–25% MVC), medium- (25–50% MVC), and high- (50–75% MVC) threshold motor units (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the clustering approach.

claim: All statistical analyses were performed using linear mixed effect models implemented in the R package lmerTest with the Kenward-Roger method.
source: All statistical analyses were performed using linear mixed effect models implemented in the R package lmerTest with the Kenward-Roger method to estimate the denominator degrees of freedom and the p-values.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the statistical methods.

claim: The significance level was set at 0.05.
source: The significance level was set at 0.05.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the significance threshold.

claim: This is the most comprehensive framework to date of motor unit activity during isometric contractions.
source: To provide the most comprehensive framework to date of motor unit activity during isometric contractions, we identified the firing activity of extensive samples of motor units in the tibialis anterior (129 ± 44 per participant; n=8) and the vastus lateralis (130 ± 63 per participant; n=8) muscles during isometric contractions of up to 80% of maximal force.
evidence: The manuscript makes this claim in the abstract based on the scope of data collected.

claim: The rate coding of each motor unit was characterised as the relation between its instantaneous firing rate and the applied force.
source: From this unique dataset, the rate coding of each motor unit was characterised as the relation between its instantaneous firing rate and the applied force, with the assumption that the linear increase in isometric force reflects a proportional increase in the net synaptic excitatory inputs received by the motoneuron.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the characterization approach.

claim: The relation between firing rate and force was characterised with a natural logarithm function that comprised two stages.
source: This relation was characterised with a natural logarithm function that comprised two stages.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional characterization.

claim: The initial stage was marked by a steep acceleration of firing rate, which was greater for low- than medium- and high-threshold motor units.
source: The initial stage was marked by a steep acceleration of firing rate, which was greater for low- than medium- and high-threshold motor units.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings in the abstract.

claim: The second stage comprised a linear increase in firing rate, which was greater for high- than medium- and low-threshold motor units.
source: The second stage comprised a linear increase in firing rate, which was greater for high- than medium- and low-threshold motor units.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings in the abstract.

claim: Changes in firing rate were largely non-linear during the ramp-up and ramp-down phases of the task.
source: Changes in firing rate were largely non-linear during the ramp-up and ramp-down phases of the task, but with significant prolonged firing activity only evident for medium-threshold motor units.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings in the abstract.

claim: Significant prolonged firing activity was only evident for medium-threshold motor units.
source: Changes in firing rate were largely non-linear during the ramp-up and ramp-down phases of the task, but with significant prolonged firing activity only evident for medium-threshold motor units.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings in the abstract.

claim: The firing rate of each motor unit can follow a large variety of trends with force across the pool, contrary to what is usually assumed.
source: Contrary to what is usually assumed, our results demonstrate that the firing rate of each motor unit can follow a large variety of trends with force across the pool.
evidence: The manuscript makes this interpretive claim in the abstract based on the findings.

claim: These findings indicate how motor unit pools use gain control to transform inputs with limited bandwidths into an intended muscle force.
source: From a neural control perspective, these findings indicate how motor unit pools use gain control to transform inputs with limited bandwidths into an intended muscle force.
evidence: The manuscript makes this interpretive claim in the abstract based on the findings.

claim: No previous studies have identified the firing activity of >100 motor units spanning most of the spectrum of recruitment thresholds from the same individual, whether in animals or humans.
source: No previous studies have identified to date the firing activity of >100 motor units spanning most of the spectrum of recruitment thresholds from the same individual, whether in animals or humans.
evidence: The manuscript makes this claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Most of the active motor units present in the recorded volume for each muscle were identified in this study.
source: We have therefore identified in this study most of the active motor units present in the recorded volume for each muscle (Figure 1), which has allowed us to infer the rate coding of pools of motor units during slow isometric contractions.
evidence: The manuscript makes this claim based on comparison with previous estimates.

claim: Motor units within a pool exhibit distinct rate coding with changes in force level, which contrasts with the long-held belief that rate coding is similar across motor units from the same pool.
source: Overall, we found that motor units within a pool exhibit distinct rate coding with changes in force level (Figures 2 and 3), which contrasts with the long-held belief that rate coding is similar across motor units from the same pool (Fuglevand et al., 1993; De Luca and Contessa, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript makes this interpretive claim based on the findings and cites contrasting literature.
